newsitem.title: CANADA: FOCUS - Canada markets drop sharply again.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Canada markets drop sharply again.

text.p: Canadian financial markets posted their third session of sharp declines in less than a week on Wednesday, with stocks, bonds and the dollar tumbling.
Analysts blamed the decline on sales by foreign investors hoping to lock in profits before year end, weaker U.S. markets and the distorting impact of thinner than usual volumes.
"It's still the end of year profit-taking," said Harvinder Kalirai, Canadian analyst with New York-based financial analysis firm I.D.E.A. "Fundamentals haven't really changed at all."

The selloff in Canadian bonds and currency began overnight, with the Canadian dollar weakening to C$1.3640 ($0.7331) overseas. Bonds were also weaker overnight and opened in Canada down C$1.45 ($1.06) to C$110.35 ($81) to yield 7.125 percent.

Canadian stocks quickly followed bonds and the dollar lower. The benchmark Toronto Stock Exchange 300 Index fell 1.2 percent at the open and closed down 138 points or 2.3 percent, its sixth biggest daily fall ever.

Bonds pared some losses to close the session down C$1.10 ($0.8074) to C$110.55 ($81.14) to yield 7.109 percent. The currency closed weaker at C$1.3608 ($0.7349) from Tuesday's close at C$1.3582 ($0.7363).

The declines followed similar sharp drops last Thursday and Friday. Thursday's activity was described as a "made-in-Canada meltdown" in which profit-taking by bond investors prompted panic selling that spilled over to the currency and stocks.

Analysts said the weakness in bonds on Wednesday morning was prompted by further foreign selling as well as weaker U.S. Treasuries. They said that profit-taking by foreign bondholders hurt the currency in turn.

"They (bond investors) are going to have to sell Canadian dollars to take it back into their own currency. The danger is you get a vicious cycle where the weaker currency feeds to the weaker bonds and the weaker bonds to the weaker currency," I.D.E.A.'s Kalirai said.

The weakness in Canadian bonds spread to the stock market on Wednesday morning, especially hurting heavily weighted financial services stocks. Shares of oil producers also fell amid a drop in oil prices.
Analysts said Canadian stocks were also hurt as portfolio managers, disturbed by recent sharp drops in the market, shifted some of their assets out of the sector.

"The scare on Friday, both in New York and in Toronto, induced portfolio managers to have a good look at their portfolios. I think that they realized that maybe it would be prudent to take some profit," said Ron Meisels, a portfolio consultant and president of Montreal-based P & C Holdings Ltd.
The TSE 300 index has gained sharply in 1996. At Tuesday's close the index was up almost 25 percent this year.
